clue.text: Mailer distributes a transatlantic fantasy

explanation.surface: Norman Mailer hands out a dream of America to his readers.
explanation.definitionFit: Norman Mailer published a 1965 novel of that title, and the phrase also names the hoped-for vision of success in the United States.

clue.text: "Good, the more /Communicated, more — grows" (Paradise Lost)

parts.note: a quotation from Milton's epic with one word blanked out, to be supplied from the poem

explanation.walkthrough: Milton's line runs: good, the more communicated, the more plentiful it grows.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is Milton's adjective for plentiful, completing the line from Book V of the poem.

clue.text: Novel appearance of Watson, seen to redden on entering Holmes's den?

definitions.text: seen to redden on entering Holmes's den

explanation.surface: Dr Watson blushes as he walks into the detective's room.
explanation.walkthrough: A den is a study, so someone who reddens on entering Holmes's den is literally in scarlet inside a study.
explanation.definitionFit: Conan Doyle's first Sherlock Holmes novel introduced Dr Watson; read literally the title describes a person blushing in a private room.

clue.text: Afflictions caused by dull prose -a token nuisance, to some extent

indicators.note: to some extent says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Tedious writing is a small but real irritation to the reader.
explanation.definitionFit: Boredom and weariness are what tedious writing inflicts, plural states of listless tedium.

clue.text: Would writer's block support the act of finality for which Nabokov issued this?

definitions.text: Would writer's block support the act of finality for which Nabokov issued this?

parts.words: Would writer's block support the act of finality for which Nabokov issued this?
parts.note: the writer's block is reimagined as an executioner's block, and Nabokov's novel title asks the reader to a beheading

explanation.surface: A question about whether a novelist's creative blockage brought a book to its end.
explanation.walkthrough: Nabokov wrote Invitation to a Beheading; the block that supports a final act is the headsman's block, not a writer's dry spell.
explanation.definitionFit: Nabokov's novel title begins with this word for a request to attend, here a request to attend an execution.

clue.text: Charitable offering for devotional songs written without afterthought

indicators.note: without tells us to take the afterthought away from the songs

parts.note: psalms are sacred songs of worship
PS, postscript, is an afterthought added to a letter

explanation.surface: Hymns written down with nothing added later make a gift to charity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes PS (postscript) from PSALMS.
explanation.definitionFit: Money or food given to the poor is the classic charitable donation.

clue.text: Barrie characters whom Arthur Quiller-Couch would have liked to see dispatched?

definitions.text: Barrie characters whom Arthur Quiller-Couch would have liked to see dispatched?

parts.words: Barrie characters whom Arthur Quiller-Couch would have liked to see dispatched?
parts.note: refers to the family in Peter Pan and to Quiller-Couch's advice that writers should murder their favourite passages

explanation.surface: Imagining one Edwardian man of letters wishing death on another's fictional family.
explanation.walkthrough: Quiller-Couch told writers to 'murder your darlings', meaning cut the passages they love; Wendy, John and Michael in Peter Pan share that surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The children in Barrie's Peter Pan bear this surname, which is also the word for cherished favourites.

clue.text: Aiken incunabulum shows planet cock-a hoop

parts.note: our planet is the Earth
cock-a-hoop means exultant, jubilant

explanation.surface: An early printed book by Aiken depicts a world in high spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: Conrad Aiken's first published collection of poems (1914) bears this title; 'incunabulum' here means an earliest work.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1914 debut volume of the American poet Conrad Aiken carries this title, his literary cradle-work.

clue.text: What Ruskin's painters are no longer

definitions.text: What Ruskin's painters are no longer

parts.words: What Ruskin's painters are no longer
parts.note: Ruskin's five-volume study had a title describing its painters as up to date, which after a century and more they are not

explanation.surface: A remark that the artists Ruskin championed have gone out of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruskin's work is titled Modern Painters; Turner and his contemporaries are now historical.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruskin's painters were called contemporary in his title, a description time has since made untrue.

clue.text: One of his plays was overheard

definitions.text: One of his plays was overheard

parts.words: One of his plays was overheard
parts.note: the playwright wrote a 1981 play whose title is the word at the end of the clue

explanation.surface: Someone eavesdropped on a dramatist's work.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Ustinov's play Overheard was staged in 1981; 'overheard' is the play's title, not a sound signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The actor and dramatist Peter Ustinov wrote a play titled Overheard.

clue.text: Additional horror, say, from usurping prince

indicators.note: say tells us to pronounce the phrase and hear another word

parts.note: more dread is extra horror

explanation.surface: Extra terror comes from a prince who seizes the throne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' signals that MORE DREAD, spoken, gives the name.
explanation.definitionFit: In Arthurian legend King Arthur's nephew seized the throne while Arthur was abroad.

clue.text: Anarchic types with a father-fixation?

parts.note: the art movement's name repeats a childish word for a parent, read as an obsession with fathers

explanation.surface: Rebels who are psychologically obsessed with their fathers.
explanation.walkthrough: The early-20th-century anti-art movement took the name Dada, which sounds like a child calling for its father.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the anarchic anti-art movement founded in Zurich in 1916.

clue.text: Sort of royalty that knew a few angles, having suffered a dolorous stroke?

definitions.text: Sort of royalty that knew a few angles, having suffered a dolorous stroke?

parts.words: Sort of royalty that knew a few angles, having suffered a dolorous stroke?
parts.note: the wounded Grail king of Arthurian legend, who passed his time angling, is the royalty meant

explanation.surface: A monarch who knew some tricks after a grievous blow.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fisher King was maimed by the Dolorous Stroke in Grail legend and spent his days fishing; 'angles' means fishing, not geometry.
explanation.definitionFit: The Fisher King is the Grail-keeper of Arthurian romance, wounded and left to fish.

clue.text: A tale of Manchester life admired by Dickens

definitions.text: A tale of Manchester life admired by Dickens

parts.words: A tale of Manchester life admired by Dickens
parts.note: the subtitle of Elizabeth Gaskell's first novel, which Dickens praised

explanation.surface: A novel set in Manchester that Dickens liked.
explanation.walkthrough: Gaskell's 1848 novel is subtitled A Tale of Manchester Life; Dickens then invited her to write for his magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth Gaskell's 1848 debut novel carries that subtitle and drew Dickens's praise.

clue.text: The French red one would be kind to 12

definitions.text: The French red one would be kind to 12

parts.words: The French red one would be kind to 12
parts.note: the French word for a dwarf, as in a red dwarf star, and the dwarf is the kind of being linked with the Grail king

explanation.surface: A French red figure who would treat the wounded king kindly.
explanation.walkthrough: In French the word means dwarf; a red dwarf is a kind of star.
explanation.definitionFit: The French noun for a dwarf, as in a red dwarf.

clue.text: What Ms Highsmith's travelling protagonists would have remained, if meeting in Britain

definitions.text: What Ms Highsmith's travelling protagonists would have remained, if meeting in Britain

parts.words: What Ms Highsmith's travelling protagonists would have remained, if meeting in Britain
parts.note: Patricia Highsmith's two rail passengers who plot murders would never have spoken on a reserved British train

explanation.surface: A thought that Highsmith's plot depended on two people chatting on a train.
explanation.walkthrough: Highsmith's novel is Strangers on a Train; British passengers famously do not talk to one another, so the pair would have stayed unacquainted.
explanation.definitionFit: Unacquainted people are what Highsmith's two passengers are called in her title.

clue.text: Biographer offers excerpt from twelve-toned fugue Dallapiccola composed

indicators.note: an excerpt is a piece taken from within, so the letters are found inside the following words

explanation.surface: A biographer takes a passage from a serial fugue by the Italian composer.
explanation.walkthrough: Dallapiccola was an Italian composer who used twelve-tone technique; 'twelve-toned' and 'composed' are surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Guedalla was a popular British writer of biographies such as Palmerston and The Duke.

clue.text: "Creeps in this petty pace from—-— —" (Macbeth)

parts.note: a line from the tomorrow-and-tomorrow speech with three words blanked out

explanation.walkthrough: Macbeth: 'Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow, creeps in this petty pace from day to day.'
explanation.definitionFit: The missing three words complete Macbeth's line about time passing one dawn after another.

clue.text: May act as writer's cover, as perhaps my pun does

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters could be arranged otherwise, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A pen name can hide an author, as a jokey wordplay may.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' tells us to rearrange MY PUN DOES.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen name is an assumed name that conceals an author's identity.

clue.text: Delacorta's French one in the Italian

indicators.note: in puts the French word inside the Italian one

parts.note: la is Italian for the (feminine)
un is French for one

explanation.surface: Delacorta's French one appears in the Italian edition.
explanation.walkthrough: Delacorta, the French author of Diva, also wrote a novel called Luna.
explanation.definitionFit: Delacorta's novel title is meant: the definition stands for his book.

clue.text: Copied badly, like last part of lyric poem

definitions.text: like last part of lyric poem

indicators.note: badly says the letters of the word are put in poor order

explanation.surface: A poorly copied version resembles a poem's closing section.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges COPIED.
explanation.definitionFit: The epode is the third, concluding section of a Pindaric ode, so this adjective describes it.

clue.text: Handsome French usurper's courtier

explanation.surface: A good-looking Frenchman serves at the court of a ruler who seized power.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means the good-looking one, and it names the courtier of the usurping Duke Frederick in Shakespeare's As You Like It.

clue.text: Sort of tartan novelist?

parts.note: the pen name of a historical novelist reads as an adjective meaning tartan-like

explanation.surface: A writer whose style resembles a checked fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: Jean Plaidy was a pen name of Eleanor Hibbert; plaid is tartan cloth, so a plaid-y thing is tartan-ish.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Plaidy was the pseudonym of a prolific British historical novelist.

clue.text: Essential equipment for a kind of wet op art

definitions.text: Essential equipment for a kind of wet op art

indicators.note: kind of signals a variant arrangement of the letters that follow

explanation.surface: A painter of watery optical art needs a basic piece of kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kind of' rearranges WET OP ART, and a pot of water is just what a watercolourist needs.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel for rinsing brushes is essential to anyone painting in watercolour.

clue.text: Iris Murdoch's was unofficial, Dorothy Parker's, perfect

explanation.surface: Two women writers compared on whether a thing was official or flawless.
explanation.definitionFit: Iris Murdoch's novel is An Unofficial Rose and Dorothy Parker's poem is One Perfect Rose, both naming the flower.

clue.text: American novelist some use as model. Illogically, perhaps

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words is used, the letters lie within them

explanation.surface: Someone takes an American novelist as a model, though perhaps without logic.
explanation.walkthrough: Don DeLillo is the American author of White Noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Don DeLillo is a leading American writer of fiction.

clue.text: Unusual breadth shown by a poet

indicators.note: unusual signals the word's letters in a strange order

explanation.surface: A poet displays remarkable broadness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' rearranges BREADTH.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare is known as the Bard, the poet par excellence.

clue.text: Enterprise issuing works like A Village Affair, Lark Rise and Mary Mitford's Country Stories?

definitions.text: Enterprise issuing works like A Village Affair, Lark Rise and Mary Mitford's Country Stories?

parts.words: Enterprise issuing works like A Village Affair, Lark Rise and Mary Mitford's Country Stories?
parts.note: these are books of rural village life, imagined as goods turned out by a home-based rustic business

explanation.surface: A business that produces books about English village life.
explanation.walkthrough: Small-scale work done at home is a cottage industry; the books named are about cottage life.
explanation.definitionFit: A small home-based business is so called, here jokingly one turning out rural fiction.
